    Import contacts

    Five columns: First Name, Last Name, Email, Phone Number, State. A row needs an email or a phone. State decides which market a contact belongs to — without one they can be stored and searched but never blasted. Full names and codes both work (California, CA, Ontario).

    Column order does not matter; headers are matched by name.

    Add market

    Leave this off for dates you have not confirmed. Unticked rows show as unverified in the list, which is what stops a send being scheduled against a guess.

    Add venue

    Josh's rule: a basketball venue hosts basketball and volleyball; a football venue hosts football, soccer, lacrosse and field hockey; a baseball venue hosts baseball and softball. There is no point inviting a football programme to a basketball venue.

    Call forwarding

    People who get a blast sometimes ring the number back. Without forwarding those calls reach nobody — there is no voicemail — so the callback is lost. Point them at one phone someone answers.     How an event becomes a blast

    The rules on this page are enforced in SQL, not by the AI. The model can reorder and veto what the rules already allowed — it can never add anything they rejected.

    1. The event exists. Schedules are pulled from each league’s own feed into the master events table, once a week per league. A season that is not published yet simply loads nothing and is picked up by the following week’s run — nobody has to remember to do it.
    2. The rules judge it. Every upcoming event is scored against the settings above. Anything that passes is Queueable; everything else carries the reason why not, which is the Eligibility column on Ticket Prices.
    3. AI Select chooses among them. You set how many markets per day and how far ahead; the AI ranks the approved candidates and may veto weak ones with a written reason. It is handed only the approved set, and every id it returns is checked back against that set before anything is written.
    4. It lands in the Queue. With copy generated per market, a sender, and a scheduled time.
    5. It leaves the Queue one of two ways. The scheduled slot fires it — but only once somebody has confirmed it. A row left pending waits however long its slot has been and gone: it is not late, it is unapproved. The other way is Send now, which fires one named row immediately and is the approval.
    6. So confirming is the gate, and leaving a blast alone holds it. Snooze moves the slot out 7 days. Reject and Archive both mean no, and they mean it on either path — a rejected or archived row is never sent, by the schedule or by a person.
    7. The chain is live. The hourly send runs, and a confirmed blast whose slot has passed goes out to real people. Demo rows are the one exception: they are marked as placeholders and are never sent automatically, whatever their status. In a non-production build, Send now is switched off as well — the button says so when that applies.

    Pricing runs on its own, shorter horizon. The scheduled refresh looks up get-in prices over , not the full send window — a price further out will have moved before the blast goes. That is why a game can be Queueable and still show no price. Games already under are not re-priced either, unless they are missing a listing link.

    Refresh prices on the Ticket Prices tab overrides that horizon for one run — you choose the number of days, and it quotes the game count and cost before spending anything. It does not change the setting the schedule uses.

    Cole Rules

    Cross-strategy fatigue warning fires under 10 days since any send to a market, regardless of strategy — a flag, not a hard block. Opt-out ceiling flags markets whose average unsubscribe rate is already running hot. Teammate AI has no game/cost fields, so it’s gated on cooldown from last-any-send only (no dedicated Teammate AI history exists yet) — no forward-window or cost/demo math applies to it.

    What the Ticket Prices columns mean

    Freshness

    How recently a price was last checked. Near-term games use a much tighter window because their prices move fastest — that is where stored prices were found running 20–25% high (AI-845). Thresholds come from the price-refresh cadence, so they change when it does.

    ShowsMeaning
    Fresh Checked recently enough to trust.
    Aging Past the point the refresh job should have re-checked it. Still usable, worth a glance.
    Stale A whole refresh cycle has been missed. These also carry a “price may be stale” badge on the Queue, because that is where a blast gets approved.
    Never priced No price stored. Expected for most games — only those inside the pricing window are looked up.
    — The game has already been played, so freshness does not apply.

    Eligibility

    Whether a blast for that event could go out right now, decided by the rules above. It answers “this price looks worth acting on — am I actually allowed to act on it?”

    ShowsMeaning
    Queueable Passes every rule — safe to blast.
    Skip — near full The event is already close to sold out, so a blast has little left to sell.
    Skip — no history No comparable blast in that market yet, so there is nothing to predict performance from.
    Hold — too early Beyond the forward-looking window set above. Most NBA and NHL games read this until their season is closer.
    Hold — cooldown That market was blasted inside the cooldown floor set above.
    not in window Not currently under consideration by the decider at all.

    A row may also carry ⚠ opt-outs running hot or ⚠ recent-send fatigue. Both are warnings, not blocks — they use the opt-out ceiling and the cross-strategy fatigue window described above.
